Just five miles from my home in West Lebanon sits an eccentric, budget-friendly local diner that feels like a slice of living history. It is the kind of unpretentious spot where charm outweighs polished decor, offering a cozy sanctuary for anyone seeking a hot meal and good company without breaking the bank.

At the heart of this quirky establishment is the owner, affectionately known simply as "H." A garrulous and lively presence, H is a devoted fan of the classic television show *Northern Exposure*—a detail that perfectly mirrors the diner’s offbeat, small-town atmosphere. H is so dedicated to the place that he practically lives behind the counter; in fact, he spends so much time at the restaurant that his wife jokingly admits she has taken to calling him by their dog's name.

Inside, the diner fosters a remarkably warm and inclusive environment. The staff greets regulars and newcomers alike with easy familiarity, and the patrons—an open-minded cross-section of the local community—are always quick to strike up a conversation. On any given day, the room hums with steady banter, usually revolving around the latest weather forecasts or stories from recent hunting trips.

The menu is a testament to authentic, unapologetic comfort food served at remarkably low prices. It skips modern culinary fads in favor of hearty, traditional fare. Breakfast features genuine, tender biscuits smothered in rich sausage gravy, while the bolder diners can opt for a local favorite: a surprisingly popular $2.25 raw hamburger dish that speaks to the menu's old-school roots.

What truly makes the diner special is how seamlessly it adapts to the routines of the community. During hunting season, the lights switch on at 4:30 a.m. to feed early risers before they head out into the woods. Yet, the establishment also knows how to host a celebration, regularly bringing locals together for special occasions like their popular New Year’s Eve seafood party. More than just an affordable place to eat, this local treasure is a vital gathering spot where West Lebanon’s unique character is served daily.
outputs.L4:
If you were to walk past the little diner tucked between the laundromat and the secondhand bookstore on Elm Street, you might mistake it for a thrift store that somehow acquired a commercial grill. There is no neon sign displaying a slick logo—just a hand-painted wooden board outside that simply reads: *H’s*. It isn't just an inexpensive place to grab a bite; at a time when a simple lunch can break the bank, H’s remains practically a public service, serving up hearty meals for a handful of pocket change. 

The interior is a glorious, chaotic mosaic of mid-century kitsch and quirky charm. No two chairs match, and the vinyl booths range in color from faded turquoise to burnt orange. The walls are an endless gallery of oddities: brass nautical clocks, vintage tin signs that buzz in a gentle, comforting hum, and a dedicated "Hall of Fame" feature wall entirely covered in framed polaroids of local dogs wearing party hats. Floating above it all is the irresistible aroma of sizzling butter, roasted coffee beans, and griddled onions.

Behind the counter stands H himself. A man whose real name remains a closely guarded neighborhood secret, H is an eccentric force of nature. Wearing his signature combination of a tilted fedora, a bright apron, and mismatched socks, he greets everyone who walks through the door with a booming, theatrical welcome. H treats short-order cooking like a mad science experiment. The menu, hand-scribbled daily on a cracked slate chalkboard, changes on a whim. While you can always get a classic, fluffiest-in-town five-dollar stack of pancakes, you are just as likely to find his daring daily creations: peanut butter and jalapeño bacon burgers, blueberry-basil grilled cheese, or his famous "Mystery Hash." Despite the unorthodox pairings, H’s culinary gambles somehow always land, resulting in food that is shockingly delicious, endlessly surprising, and endlessly comforting.

What truly transforms the diner from a quirky eatery into a beloved community haven, however, is its atmosphere. H’s is the neighborhood’s unofficial living room. On any given morning, you can find college students pulling all-nighters sitting beside retired postal workers, sharing syrup and swapping stories. H knows his regulars not just by name, but by their coffee preferences and life updates, frequently sliding free slices of homemade pie across the counter to anyone who looks like they’ve had a tough week. 

It is this fierce sense of familiarity, combined with the exciting unpredictability of H’s evolving menu, that inspires such intense loyalty among his patrons. The diner is a anchor in an ever-changing town, a place where everyone is made to feel like a VIP. 

As the year draws to a close, there is nowhere else I would rather celebrate the passage of time. H has already taped his hand-drawn flyer for the diner’s annual New Year’s Eve bash to the front window, promising a midnight balloon drop, a mystery five-course tasting menu for twelve dollars, and a sparkling cider toast. I’ve already reserved my spot at the counter, ready to ring in the new year surrounded by good food, great neighbors, and the delightful madness of H’s little world.
outputs.L5:
**It’s A Lot Like...**

“It’s a lot like...” is perhaps the most human phrase in our language. It is the universal opening line for translation—not from one language to another, but from one person’s internal world to another’s. We reach for it whenever we are faced with the impossible task of explaining the unexplainable. 

How do you describe falling in love to someone who has never felt it? You don’t offer a clinical definition of dopamine and oxytocin. Instead, you say, *“It’s a lot like stepping off a high ledge into warm water.”* 

How do you explain grief? You say, *“It’s a lot like carrying a heavy stone in your pocket. At first, it weighs you down so much you can barely walk. Over time, the stone doesn't get any lighter, but your hands just get stronger.”*

We use this phrase as verbal scaffolding. When the terrain of a new experience is too rocky or unfamiliar, we build a bridge out of things we already know. It is how we learn, how we teach, and how we comfort one another. A teacher explaining the structure of an atom will say it’s a lot like a miniature solar system. A friend describing a panic attack will say it’s a lot like drowning in mid-air. 

There is a quiet beauty in the word *“like.”* It acknowledges an inherent truth: no two experiences are identical, but they can be adjacent. Saying "it's a lot like" is an invitation rather than a declaration. It leaves room for nuance. It says, *“My experience isn’t exactly yours, but if you look through this lens, you might see what I see.”*

Growing up, changing careers, losing a dream, or discovering a new passion—life rarely gives us a neat instruction manual. Instead, it gives us analogies. 

Navigating adulthood, after all, is a lot like driving down a dark highway at night. You can only see as far as your headlights project, but if you just keep moving forward, you can make the entire journey that way. 

In the end, “it’s a lot like” is empathy’s favorite shortcut. It is our way of reaching out in the dark, tapping someone on the shoulder, and reassuring them: *You haven't been here before, but you already understand more than you think.*

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a short prose vignette about a local, eccentric greasy spoon diner in a stream-of-consciousness, informal style.
counterfactuals.output: Duct tape on the third booth red vinyl split right down the middle like a surgical scar and God it smells like burnt butter and thirty years of bad decisions, scuffed linoleum, scorched Folgers bubbling in the glass pot that Marcie’s been slinging since the Carter administration. She doesn’t even ask, just slaps down a heavy white mug thick as a brick, *clack*, coffee black as coal tar pouring in before I even get my coat off, "You're looking ragged hon," thanks Marcie love you too. Look at Artie behind the flat top—guy’s wearing a tank top underneath an apron that’s more grease than cotton, scraping the iron with a drywall spatula, *shhh-t, shhh-t*, flipping hash browns with the casual disinterest of a man who has transcended breakfast. Neon sign in the window buzzing like a trapped hornet, *EAT*, just says *EAT*, the *AT JOE’S* part burned out back in ’04 and nobody bothered, why bother, everybody knows where they are anyway. Wall’s covered in framed polaroids of dogs that don’t exist anymore and a stuffed smallmouth bass wearing a clip-on tie. Why the tie? Don’t ask. Old Man Jenkins over in booth one reading three different newspapers at the same time, shuffling the sports section into the obituaries, muttering about soybean futures, radio in the kitchen stuck between an oldies station and static so Patsy Cline sounds like she’s singing from the bottom of a well. The salt shaker’s sticky. The pepper shaker’s sticky. Everything has a micro-coating of lard and love and yellowed light, but the butter—real butter, none of that tub margarine crap—is currently melting into a stack of buttermilk cakes so thick they could stop a bullet. You hit the bottom of the glass ketchup bottle on the number 57 just right or you don’t get any at all, that's the law here, time stopped somewhere around nineteen-ninety-two and honestly, slide me another slice of pie, why would anyone ever want to leave?

counterfactuals.prompt: Describe your favorite local dive restaurant in lowercase prose poem format. Focus on quirky details about the owner, cheap food options like a $2.25 raw hamburger with an egg yolk, hunting season hours, and the overall atmosphere.
counterfactuals.output:
the front door hangs sideways on a single brass hinge, holding back thirty years of griddle smoke and the low hum of a faulty neon bass that flickers whenever the freight train rolls past. a cardboard sign in the grease-filmed window doesn't give normal hours, it just says *closed for deer season, open when the freezer is full*, written in faded permanent marker over a calendar from 1994. but when the season ends, the deadbolts slide back at four in the morning for the men in camouflage who smell like pine cover-spray, sliding into olive-green vinyl booths patched with duct tape that peels against the back of your jeans. 

artie stands behind the counter wearing a grease-stained apron over a sleeveless flannel, his left eyebrow permanently hooked high while he argues about 1980s baseball statistics with a muted tube television. he keeps a plastic bucket of pickled pigs' feet floating like pale specimens beside the register, and he stores his extra reading glasses in an empty mustard jar. the menu is just a yellowed piece of cardstock pinned to the wall with a bent nail, offering fifty-cent black coffee poured from a dented pot and the famous two-dollar-and-twenty-five-cent raw hamburger special—a cold ball of freshly ground chuck served open-faced on a slice of store-bought white bread, crowned with a single, trembling raw egg yolk that sits like a yellow sun waiting to be popped by a plastic fork. 

the linoleum is worn straight down to the grey plywood path where artie paces between the flat top and the counter, muttering soft coaxing words to a blind, hairless chihuahua that sleeps inside an old crockpot box under the fry station. a layer of seasoned grease coats the wood-paneled walls like a varnish of pure comfort, catching the amber glare of a flickering beer sign while the ancient jukebox stuck on a loop skips over the same line of a johnny cash song, and no one ever complains, because here in the warm and sticky dark, two dollars and twenty-five cents still buys you breakfast and a front-row seat to the end of the world.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an unpolished, conversational description of a rural diner in upstate New York, mentioning high-caffeine coffee, pinball machines, local regulars, and genuine biscuits with sausage gravy.
counterfactuals.output:
Look, if you’re driving way up past Saratoga—like, where the cell service drops to one bar and every second truck has a snowplow rig attached to it—you gotta pull into Dot’s. It basically looks like a rusty silver diner car that someone slapped a screen door onto back in 1982, sitting in a gravel lot full of muddy F-150s. 

Walk in, and it just smells like bacon grease, wet wool, and old wood paneling. The counter is completely taken over by the regulars. Same four guys in Carhartt jackets every single morning, sipping out of chipped mugs, complaining about the town council or how early the frost came in this year. The waitress knows all of them by name and just slides them refills without even asking. 

Speaking of coffee—holy shit. It’s not fancy, just whatever black drip they brewed at 4:30 AM, but it’s like jet fuel. I’m pretty sure they scoop pure caffeine into the grounds because two sips of that piping hot sludge and your eyelids start twitching. It’ll burn your tongue off, but man, it gets you awake fast.

Off in the back corner right near the bathrooms, they’ve got these two ancient pinball machines. The left flipper on the *Addams Family* one is super sticky and the backglass lighting is half-dead, but there’s almost always some guy in boots leaning over it, dropping quarters in while his food cools off. So the whole morning just has this background rhythm of griddle scrapers, muffled gossip, and *ding-ding-ding-buzz*.

You go there for the biscuits and gravy, though. No question. It's not that pale, gluey canned garbage you get at chains. These are actual homemade buttermilk biscuits, big as a softball and flaky as hell, covered in this heavy, peppery sausage gravy that’s got huge, jagged chunks of local pork in it. Looks like absolute gray sludge on the plate, honestly, but it is the real deal. Eat a plate of that with a cup of the jet-fuel coffee and you basically don't need to eat again until tomorrow.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Can you write a realistic journal-style entry detailing a beloved local diner run by a chatty owner with suspenders, including funny details like his wife calling him by the dog's name and plans for a New Year's Eve seafood dinner there?
counterfactuals.output:
**December 28th**

If my apartment building burned down, the only thing I’d truly mourn—besides my hard drive—is my proximity to *Pete’s Clocktower Diner*. It’s only three blocks away, but walking in there on a freezing morning like today feels like stepping straight into a warm, butter-scented hug. 

I took my usual spot at the counter around 8:30. Pete was already mid-monologue, snapping his bright red suspenders against his plaid shirt for emphasis. I don’t think those suspenders actually hold his pants up; I think they’re just tactical handles for when he needs to stretch and snap them to highlight a point. Today’s rant was about the city’s new snowplow routes, which he claims were designed by "a drunk squirrel." 

Pete is sixty-four, has the vocal capacity of a foghorn, and cannot physically stop talking. If you sit at the counter, you are his captive audience. I got a full fifteen-minute history of the local hardware store’s inventory changes since 1991 while my eggs were cooking.

The highlight of the morning, though, was his wife, Velma. 

Velma works the kitchen pass-through and the cash register, serving as the quiet, deadpan anchor to Pete’s floating balloon of hot air. Pete was in the middle of explaining to an exhausted-looking truck driver why instant coffee is a sign of societal collapse, when Velma’s head popped out from behind the heat lamps. 

"Barnaby!" she yelled over the sizzle of the grill. "Stop barking at the customers and get the lady her side of turkey sausage!"

Pete didn’t even flinch. He just grabbed the plate, slid it across to me, and yelled back, "I'm working on it, Vel!" 

The truck driver looked confused, but I had to bite the inside of my cheek to keep from laughing into my mug. *Barnaby* is their ancient, three-legged Beagle who spends twenty hours a day sleeping on a dog bed next to the ice machine. Pete has been answering to the dog's name for at least five years now, and I honestly don't think he even notices anymore. Or maybe he just accepts his place in the pack. 

Before I left, Pete slapped a neon-pink paper flyer down on the counter in front of me with a proud *thwack*. 

"Big news," he announced, hooking his thumbs under his suspenders. "We’re doing fancy this year. New Year’s Eve. Four-course Seafood Extravaganza. Reservations only."

I looked at the flyer. It had a piece of clipart featuring a lobster wearing a top hat. 

Now, Pete’s Diner is famous for two things: home fries crispier than a autumn leaf, and a coffee pot that has been brewing continuously since the Bush administration. "Seafood Extravaganza" feels like a dangerous game for a place whose fish options usually begin and end with Friday night cod sticks. 

"Fresh clams," Pete whispered dramatically, leaning over the counter like a man dealing black-market diamonds. "Velma’s making her legendary crab dip. I got a guy in Maine flying in actual lobsters. We’re putting tablecloths down, kid. *Cloth* ones. Not the vinyl."

I couldn't resist. I signed up on the yellow legal pad he handed me. I’m reservation #4 for 7:00 PM on the 31st. 

Sarah thinks I’m insane to eat seafood at a greasy spoon on New Year’s Eve, but I wouldn’t miss it for the world. Seeing Pete in a bowtie over his suspenders, watching Velma try to keep him from dropping a lobster into the deep fryer, and drinking champagne out of thick ceramic coffee mugs sounds a hundred times better than paying $150 at some cramped downtown lounge. 

Counting down the days. I just hope Barnaby—the dog, not Pete—doesn't eat the crab dip first.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Describe a cheap, quirky restaurant five miles from your house where you go when you have almost no money, capturing all the oddities of the place, its owner, and the regulars.
counterfactuals.output:
Exactly five miles down the cracked asphalt of the Old Industrial Parkway—past the auto salvage yard and the overgrown mini-golf course—sits **Gus’s Clockwork & Cabaret**. 

It is neither a clock shop nor a cabaret. It is an illegally retrofitted Waffle House from the mid-1970s that serves an unclassifiable menu of pan-Asian street food, Southern greasy-spoon staples, and whatever Gus managed to buy in bulk at the wholesale outlet that morning. When my bank account dips below single digits, this is my sanctuary. 

The building itself looks like a fever dream. The classic yellow-tiled roof remains, but Gus has painted the exterior a blinding neon magenta. The front window bears two glowing neon signs: one says *OPEN*, and the other—stolen from a long-defunct dry cleaner—says *SAME DAY SUITS*. 

Inside, the air smells intensely of toasted sesame oil, scorched black coffee, and old paper. The decor is dominated by Gus’s primary obsession: horology. Every square inch of wall space is covered in mismatched wall clocks—cuckoo clocks, plastic cat clocks with wagging tails, brass ship’s wheels, and bank digital displays. None of them are set to the correct time, and only about half of them tick, creating an erratic, rain-like rhythm of *clack-tick-tock* that somehow lulls you into a trance. The vinyl booths are a rainbow of duct-tape repair jobs, green on orange, red on blue.

The owner, Gus, is a seventy-year-old Greek man who wears high-top Converse, a velvet vest over a Hawaiian shirt, and jeweler’s loupes pushed up onto his bald head. Gus doesn't give you a menu. If you sit down, he assesses your spiritual and financial wreckage with a quick glance over his bifocals. 

"You look broke," he’ll say, dropping a chipped mug of diner coffee in front of you. "You got five dollars?"

If you hand him five crumpled bills, he disappears behind a kitchen swinging door that has a life-sized poster of Bruce Lee taped to it. Ten minutes later, he emerges with the "Special." It is always a mountain of food served on a chipped, floral-patterned plate: usually a massive bed of garlic fried rice topped with two over-easy eggs, three crispy pork dumplings, and a side of home fries soaked in hot sauce. It costs $4.50. He lets you keep the fifty cents change "for the jukebox," which only plays 1980s synth-pop and Spanish-language polka.

The regulars are as much a part of the architecture as the ticking walls.

In the corner booth sits Sal, known locally as "The Mayor." Sal wears a trench coat regardless of the season and spends twelve hours a day solving crosswords from discarded newspapers. He hasn't ordered food since 2018; he simply pays Gus fifty cents every two hours for infinite coffee refills and acts as the house philosopher, shouting unsolicited advice to anyone entering the bathroom. 

At the counter sits Vee, a night-shift welder with fluorescent purple hair and a tattoo of a stapler on her neck. Vee trades hand-drawn caricature sketches of the shop’s clocks on paper napkins in exchange for Gus’s scallion pancakes. 

Then there is Brother Ray, a gentleman of indeterminate age who wears a tuxedo jacket over sweatpants. Ray claims to be a retired magician from Atlantic City. If you look sad while eating your budget rice, Ray will shuffle over, pull a greasy quarter from behind your ear, drop it into your palm, and walk away without saying a word.

Eating at Gus’s is an exercise in surreal comfort. There are no avocado toasts, no QR-code menus, and certainly no health department certificates newer than 2019 displayed with any prominence. But when you have $6.00 to your name, the world feels cold, and your bank app is a horror show, five miles is a small price to drive. You sit under the chaotic ticking of fifty wrong clocks, eat a week’s worth of carbs for the price of a latte, and for an hour, the absolute weirdness of the place makes your own life feel just a little bit more manageable.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
